name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q01 - Levels of biodiversity and global species estimates

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements regarding biodiversity and its global estimates, and identify the correct combination:

(I) Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges exhibits genetic diversity in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine.
(II) India possesses more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
(III) According to Robert May's conservative and scientifically sound estimate, the global species diversity is about 20 to 50 million.
(IV) Among the currently recorded species, the number of fungi species in the world exceeds the combined total of species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity encompasses genetic, species, and ecological diversity, and global species richness is evaluated using scientifically sound taxonomic extrapolations rather than extreme guesses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Genetic Diversity in Rauwolfia vomitoria and Indian Crops
The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing across different Himalayan ranges shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of reserpine it produces. Similarly, India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango, both representing high genetic diversity. Hence, both propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Robert May's Global Estimate
Extreme estimates of global species diversity range from 20 to 50 million, whereas Robert May placed the more conservative and scientifically sound estimate of global species diversity at about 7 million. Therefore, attributing 20 to 50 million to Robert May is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Fungi Species Richness
Based on currently available species inventories, the number of fungi species in the world is greater than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals. Thus, this proposition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding Rauwolfia vomitoria, Indian rice and mango varieties, and global fungi richness are correct, while the proposition attributing 20 to 50 million to Robert May is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q02 - Global species proportions and India's biodiversity share

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements about global and Indian species inventories and select the correct set of statements:

(I) More than 70 per cent of all recorded species are animals, whereas plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total.
(II) Conventional taxonomic methods are well-suited for identifying all prokaryotic species, making their global species count accurately known.
(III) Although India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, its share of global species diversity is 8.1 per cent.
(IV) Applying Robert May's global estimate proportion (22 per cent recorded), more than 1,00,000 plant species and more than 3,00,000 animal species are yet to be discovered in India.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Species inventories compare taxonomic proportions across animals, plants, and microbes, and allow estimation of undiscovered biodiversity in mega-diversity nations like India.

Step 2: Evaluation of Animal and Plant Proportions
Among all recorded species, animals constitute more than 70 per cent (with insects making up over 70 per cent of animals), while plants (broadly grouped to include algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent. This proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Prokaryotic Taxonomic Estimates
Biologists are uncertain about the number of prokaryotic species because conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species, and many microbes cannot be cultured under laboratory conditions. Therefore, claiming that conventional methods make prokaryotic counts accurately known is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of India's Land Area, Diversity Share, and Undiscovered Species
India accounts for only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area yet holds an impressive 8.1 per cent of global species diversity, making it one of the 12 mega-diversity countries. With nearly 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species recorded, and assuming only 22 per cent of total species are recorded per May's estimate, more than 1,00,000 plant species and more than 3,00,000 animal species remain to be discovered and described in India. Both propositions are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning animal-plant proportions, India's 2.4 per cent land area and 8.1 per cent diversity share, and India's undiscovered plant and animal species are correct, whereas the proposition on prokaryotic taxonomy is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q03 - Latitudinal gradients and species area relationship

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding patterns of biodiversity and choose the correct option:

(I) Species diversity generally decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles, with Colombia near the equator harbouring nearly 1,400 bird species compared to 56 in Greenland.
(II) Tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and leads to greater species diversity.
(III) On a logarithmic scale, the species-area relationship \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\) represents a rectangular hyperbola, whereas on an arithmetic scale it forms a straight line.
(IV) For very large areas such as entire continents, the slope of the regression line \(Z\) lies in the range of 0.6 to 1.2, which is much steeper than the 0.1 to 0.2 range observed for smaller regions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity exhibits predictable spatial patterns, notably latitudinal gradients from the tropics to the poles and Alexander von Humboldt's species-area relationship.

Step 2: Evaluation of Latitudinal Gradients and Tropical Stability
Species richness declines from the equator towards the poles: Colombia near the equator has nearly 1,400 bird species, New York at \(41^{\circ}\text{ N}\) has 105, and Greenland at \(71^{\circ}\text{ N}\) has only 56. Furthermore, tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively constant, and predictable, promoting niche specialisation and higher species diversity. Both of these propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Species-Area Graph Shape
On an arithmetic scale, the relation between species richness \(S\) and area \(A\) (\(S = CA^{Z}\)) turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola. When plotted on a logarithmic scale, the equation \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\) yields a straight line. Reversing these two curve shapes makes the proposition incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Regression Coefficient \(Z\)
For smaller regions and specific taxa (such as plants in Britain or birds in California), \(Z\) typically lies between 0.1 and 0.2. However, when analysing very large areas like entire continents, the slope becomes much steeper, with \(Z\) values ranging from 0.6 to 1.2 (for example, 1.15 for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents). Thus, this proposition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions on latitudinal bird diversity, tropical niche specialisation, and continental \(Z\) values are correct, while the proposition reversing the arithmetic and logarithmic shapes of the species-area curve is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q04 - Ecosystem stability Tilman experiments and rivet popper hypothesis

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements regarding the importance of species diversity to ecosystem functioning and identify the correct combination:

(I) A stable biological community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year and must be either resistant or resilient to occasional natural or man-made disturbances.
(II) David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments showed that plots with more species exhibited less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher productivity.
(III) In Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis, loss of rivets on the seats or windows of an airplane poses a more serious threat to flight safety than loss of rivets on the wings.
(IV) A stable biological community must also be resistant to invasions by alien species.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ecosystem stability depends on consistent productivity, resistance or resilience to disturbances, and resistance to biological invasions, as supported by ecological experiments and analogies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Community Stability Attributes
A stable biological community does not show excessive year-to-year variation in productivity, is resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and is resistant to invasions by alien species. Both propositions describing these stability attributes are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of David Tilman's Experiments
David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots demonstrated that plots with higher species diversity showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity. Therefore, this proposition is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Rivet Popper Hypothesis
In Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis, the airplane represents an ecosystem and the rivets represent species. Loss of rivets on the wings (representing key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is a far more serious threat to flight safety than the loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane. Reversing this comparison makes the proposition incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing the three attributes of a stable community and David Tilman's experimental findings are correct, whereas the proposition reversing the critical role of wing rivets in the rivet popper hypothesis is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q05 - Biodiversity loss extinction rates and consequences

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding the loss of biodiversity and select the correct combination:

(I) The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species in the last 500 years, including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, and 87 plants.
(II) Careful analysis of extinction records shows that extinctions across taxa are completely random, with all taxonomic groups being equally vulnerable.
(III) The current 'Sixth Extinction' differs from the previous five mass extinctions primarily in its rate, which is estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times.
(IV) Loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought and increased variability in ecosystem processes like water use and pest cycles.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modern biodiversity loss is documented by the IUCN Red List, shows taxonomic selectivity, proceeds at an unprecedented anthropogenic rate, and impairs ecosystem functioning.

Step 2: Evaluation of IUCN Red List (2004) Data
The IUCN Red List (2004) records the extinction of 784 species over the last 500 years, comprising 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, and 87 plants (such as the dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller's Sea Cow, and three subspecies of tiger). This proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Taxonomic Vulnerability to Extinction
Analysis of extinction records reveals that extinctions across taxa are not random; certain groups such as amphibians appear to be much more vulnerable to extinction than others (with 32 per cent of all amphibian species facing the threat of extinction). Therefore, claiming extinctions are completely random across taxa is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Sixth Extinction Rate and Ecosystem Consequences
Unlike the five previous episodes of mass extinction in Earth's history, the ongoing Sixth Extinction is occurring at a rate estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times due to human activities. Furthermore, biodiversity loss in a region can cause a decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought, and increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles. Both propositions are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions on the IUCN Red List (2004) figures, the accelerated rate of the Sixth Extinction, and the ecological consequences of biodiversity loss are correct, while the proposition claiming random extinctions across taxa is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q06 - The Evil Quartet causes of biodiversity losses

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements concerning 'The Evil Quartet'—the major causes of biodiversity losses—and identify the correct set:

(I) Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, but now cover no more than 6 per cent, with the Amazon rain forest being cleared for soya bean cultivation and cattle grazing.
(II) The extinctions of Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon in the last 500 years were primarily caused by alien species invasions.
(III) The introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria in east Africa led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
(IV) Co-extinction occurs when an obligatory host-parasite relationship or a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism breaks down following the extinction of one partner.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four major human-driven causes of biodiversity loss ('The Evil Quartet') are habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions, and co-extinctions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Habitat Loss in Tropical Rain Forests
Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving species to extinction. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of Earth's land surface and now cover no more than 6 per cent; the Amazon rain forest ('lungs of the planet') is being cleared for cultivating soya beans or converting to grasslands for raising beef cattle. This proposition is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Steller's Sea Cow and Passenger Pigeon Extinctions
Many species extinctions in the last 500 years, specifically Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon, occurred due to over-exploitation by humans when need turned to greed, rather than alien species invasions. Therefore, attributing their extinctions to alien species invasions is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Alien Species Invasions and Co-extinctions
The deliberate or unintentional introduction of invasive alien species can eliminate native species; for instance, introducing the Nile perch into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of more than 200 species of native cichlid fish. Likewise, co-extinction happens when species associated in an obligatory manner—such as a host fish and its unique parasites, or a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism—perish together when one becomes extinct. Both propositions are correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions on tropical rain forest habitat loss, Nile perch invasion in Lake Victoria, and co-extinctions are correct, whereas the proposition attributing the extinctions of Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon to alien invasions is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q07 - Biodiversity conservation strategies in situ and ex situ

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding biodiversity conservation and choose the correct option:

(I) Bioprospecting involves exploring molecular, genetic, and species-level diversity for products of economic importance, aligning with the narrowly utilitarian argument.
(II) Globally, 34 biodiversity hotspots covering less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area have been identified, and their strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.
(III) Sacred groves found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya and the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan are examples of ex situ conservation.
(IV) Cryopreservation of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture propagation, and seed banks are advanced methods of ex situ conservation.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity conservation is justified on utilitarian and ethical grounds and is implemented through on-site (in situ) ecosystem protection and off-site (ex situ) preservation of threatened organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bioprospecting and Biodiversity Hotspots
The narrowly utilitarian argument highlights direct economic benefits from nature, including 'bioprospecting'—exploring molecular, genetic, and species-level diversity for economically valuable products. Furthermore, 34 biodiversity hotspots (regions of high species richness, endemism, and accelerated habitat loss) cover less than 2 per cent of Earth's land area, yet their strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent. Both propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Sacred Groves
Sacred groves are tracts of forest set aside and venerated within their natural setting where all trees and wildlife receive total protection, such as in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya and the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan. Because protection occurs within the natural habitat, sacred groves are examples of in situ conservation, not ex situ conservation. Hence, this proposition is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Advanced Ex Situ Methods
Beyond zoological parks, botanical gardens, and wildlife safari parks, modern ex situ conservation includes cryopreservation of gametes in viable and fertile condition, in vitro fertilisation of eggs, tissue culture propagation of plants, and long-term storage of seeds in seed banks. Thus, this proposition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding bioprospecting, the 34 biodiversity hotspots, and advanced ex situ techniques are correct, while the proposition classifying sacred groves as ex situ conservation is incorrect.
